scenario_stem:
Foxbury Flour Mills is a private limited company in Country X, founded 9 years ago by siblings Dana and Cole Foxbury. It mills wheat into flour for 60 bakeries across the region, employing 24 millers and drivers, and last year milled 9,000 tonnes of flour. The company uses cost-plus pricing, applying a 25% markup to a production cost that has risen from $0.80 per kilogram to $0.88 and now $0.96.

The cost-plus price has therefore moved from $1.00 to $1.10 per kilogram. Keeping the 25% markup would lift the price to $1.20. Rival Harborpoint Flour sells at $1.15 per kilogram, and two large bakeries warned they will switch suppliers if prices rise again. Cole wants to hold at $1.10 and absorb the extra cost, while Dana wants the full increase passed on. The directors must decide within one month.

questions.question_text: Define 'cost-plus pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Cost-plus pricing is a pricing method in which a business calculates the total cost of producing a product and then adds a percentage markup to set the selling price. This ensures all production costs are covered and a profit margin is built in [2].

knowledge_max_2: Business calculates the total cost of making the product
Adds a percentage markup to the cost to set the selling price

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Foxbury Flour Mills uses cost-plus pricing.
questions.model_answer: Cost-plus pricing ensures that all production costs are covered and a profit is made [k], which is vital when wheat costs have risen from $0.80 to $0.96 per kilogram [app]. It is also straightforward to calculate and easy to update as costs change [k], as shown by the price moving from $1.00 to $1.10 per kilogram and possibly to $1.20 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Covers production costs and guarantees a profit margin
Simple to calculate and adjust when costs change
application_max_2: Wheat cost has risen from $0.80 to $0.88 and now $0.96 per kilogram
Price moved from $1.00 to $1.10 per kilogram and could rise to $1.20 with the 25% markup

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Foxbury Flour Mills may face if it raises its price to $1.20 per kilogram.
questions.model_answer: A higher price could make Foxbury uncompetitive against rivals [k], because Harborpoint Flour sells at $1.15 per kilogram [app], so the two large bakeries may switch suppliers, cutting Foxbury's sales volume [an]. A price rise could also damage Foxbury's relationships with long-standing customers [k], as two of its 60 bakery buyers have already warned they will switch [app], leaving capacity under-used across the 9,000 tonnes milled and reducing revenue [an].

knowledge_max_2: May become uncompetitive / rivals may be cheaper
May damage customer relationships / lose goodwill and long-standing buyers
application_max_2: Harborpoint Flour sells at $1.15 per kilogram, below the proposed $1.20
Two of Foxbury's 60 bakery customers have already warned they will switch suppliers
analysis_max_2: Sales volume and revenue fall if bakeries switch to Harborpoint
Under-used milling capacity across the 9,000 tonnes milled reduces recovery of fixed costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Foxbury Flour Mills should raise its price to $1.20 per kilogram, in line with cost-plus pricing, or hold the price at $1.10 per kilogram? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising the price to $1.20 maintains the 25% markup on the higher wheat cost of $0.96 [k], preserving the profit Foxbury earns on each of its 9,000 tonnes of flour [app], protecting cash flow and avoiding erosion of margins [an]. However, holding at $1.10 keeps Foxbury close to Harborpoint Flour's $1.15 price [k], helping Foxbury retain its 60 bakery customers and avoid losing the two large buyers who warned they will switch [app], protecting long-term revenue and market share [an]. Overall, the stronger position is to raise the price in line with cost-plus pricing [eval], because repeated input cost rises from $0.80 through $0.88 to $0.96 cannot be absorbed indefinitely without destroying profit, and the price must reflect true costs to remain sustainable [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Cost-plus keeps the markup intact and protects profit
Holding the price protects share and keeps the price close to the rival
application_max_2: $0.96 wheat cost with 25% markup gives $1.20; margin must cover 9,000 tonnes
Holding at $1.10 stays near Harborpoint Flour at $1.15; two of 60 bakeries threatening to switch
analysis_max_2: Raising preserves margin and protects cash flow
Holding protects long-term volume, share and customer relationships
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation that costs rose repeatedly ($0.80 to $0.88 to $0.96) so absorption is unsustainable
Acknowledges the risk of losing the two large bakery buyers and weighs it against margin protection

scenario_stem:
Harborview Electrical is a private limited company in Country X, founded 6 years ago by owner Priya Nair. It sells televisions, refrigerators and small appliances from two high-street shops, employing 16 staff including delivery drivers. Last year it sold 2,400 televisions at an average price of $599 against a unit cost of $410, generating $1.44 million in revenue and a profit of $0.30 million.

National chain ValueMart has cut its television prices to $549 and runs match-any-price weekend promotions. Priya can either hold $599 and rely on free delivery and expert advice, or lower to $549 to match ValueMart. Matching cuts Harborview's profit margin per television from $189 to $139, and she fears sales could fall by 20% if the higher price is held. She must set the television price for the key summer trading period.

questions.question_text: Define 'competitive pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Competitive pricing is a pricing method where a business sets its prices at or close to the prices charged by its competitors, rather than basing the price only on its own costs, so that it remains attractive to customers in the market [2].

knowledge_max_2: Price is set at or close to competitors' prices
Focus is on matching the market rather than the business's own costs

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of competitive pricing for Harborview Electrical.
questions.model_answer: Competitive pricing keeps Harborview's televisions attractive next to ValueMart, which has cut prices to $549 [k], helping Harborview defend its position against a rival running match-any-price weekend promotions [app]. It also helps prevent losing customers to cheaper competitors [k], protecting Harborview's 2,400 television sales and $1.44 million annual revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: Keeps the product attractive against rivals' prices
Helps prevent loss of customers to cheaper competitors
application_max_2: ValueMart has cut television prices to $549 and runs match-any-price weekends
Harborview sold 2,400 televisions and earned $1.44 million in revenue last year

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of competitive pricing for Harborview Electrical.
questions.model_answer: Matching ValueMart at $549 cuts the profit margin per television from $189 to $139 [k], meaning $50 is lost on every set while the cost stays at $410 [app], squeezing Harborview's $0.30 million profit across its 2,400 sales [an]. Competitive pricing also makes Harborview dependent on rivals' decisions [k], so ValueMart's match-any-price weekends may force repeated price cuts [app], eroding margins in the two shops without any guarantee of extra volume [an].

knowledge_max_2: Margins are squeezed because price is set by rivals
The business becomes dependent on competitors' pricing decisions
application_max_2: Matching $549 cuts the margin from $189 to $139 against a $410 unit cost
ValueMart runs match-any-price weekend promotions
analysis_max_2: Profit is squeezed across the 2,400 televisions sold, threatening the $0.30 million profit
Repeated reactive price cuts erode margins without guaranteeing more volume

questions.question_text: Do you think Harborview Electrical should lower its television price to $549 to match ValueMart, or hold at $599? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Matching at $549 would cut the profit margin per television from $189 to $139 [k], reducing profit on the 2,400 sets sold and threatening the $0.30 million annual profit [app], limiting funds available for the free-delivery offer and in-store advice [an]. However, holding $599 risks losing customers to ValueMart and its match-any-price weekend promotions [k], potentially cutting television sales by the 20% Priya fears across the two shops [app], shrinking Harborview's market share in its local market [an]. Overall, the stronger position is to hold at $599 but add clearer value such as free delivery and expert advice [eval], because matching a national chain's discount triggers a price war Harborview cannot win on size, while superior service justifies the $50 premium for local buyers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Matching protects volume but erodes margin per unit
Holding the price risks losing customers / market share to the rival
application_max_2: Margin falls from $189 to $139 at $549 against $410 cost
2,400 televisions sold, $0.30 million profit, ValueMart match-any-price weekends, 20% feared sales fall
analysis_max_2: Matching funds shrink (delivery, advice) and erodes per-unit margin
Holding risks sales volume and local market share
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation balancing margin erosion against share loss
Recognises Harborview cannot win a price war on size against a national chain, so service must carry the premium

scenario_stem:
Turnbridge Fitness Centre is a new private limited company in Country X, opened 4 months ago by owner Marcus Yuen. It offers a gym, pool and studio classes with capacity for 1,500 members and employs 22 full-time trainers and reception staff. Rival Capital Fitness charges $45 per month, has 900 members, and Turnbridge has spent $80,000 on launch advertising so far.

To attract members quickly, Marcus is considering penetration pricing: $25 per month for the first 3 months, after which membership rises to $42 per month. The centre has just 240 members against a year-end target of 600 and needs to build loyalty quickly. His business partner prefers launching at the standard $42 price to protect profit margins, while Marcus wants the low launch price to undercut Capital Fitness and fill the gym fast.

questions.question_text: Define 'penetration pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Penetration pricing is a pricing method where a new product or business is launched at a low price to attract customers quickly and gain market share, with the price usually rising later once the product is established [2].

knowledge_max_2: Launch price is set low to attract customers quickly
Aim is to gain market share, with price typically rising later

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of penetration pricing for Turnbridge Fitness Centre.
questions.model_answer: Penetration pricing attracts customers quickly and builds market share [k], helping Turnbridge move from just 240 members towards its year-end target of 600 [app]. The low opening price of $25 per month also undercuts Capital Fitness's $45 price [k], giving price-sensitive customers a clear incentive to switch or join [app].

knowledge_max_2: Attracts customers quickly / builds market share fast
Low price undercuts rivals and attracts price-sensitive customers
application_max_2: Turnbridge has only 240 members versus a year-end target of 600
$25 per month undercuts Capital Fitness at $45 per month

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of penetration pricing for Turnbridge Fitness Centre.
questions.model_answer: A low launch price reduces the profit made on each member [k], since $25 per month earns $17 less than the standard $42 price [app], leaving Turnbridge less able to recover its $80,000 launch advertising spend quickly [an]. Customers attracted by the offer may also leave when the price rises to $42 [k], so Turnbridge risks losing members after the 3-month offer ends [app], making membership income and cash flow unpredictable [an].

knowledge_max_2: Profit per customer is reduced by the low price
Customers may leave when the price later rises
application_max_2: $25 per month earns $17 less than the $42 standard price
$80,000 launch advertising spend and a 3-month offer period
analysis_max_2: Slower recovery of the $80,000 launch spend squeezes cash flow
Post-offer churn makes membership income and cash flow unpredictable

questions.question_text: Do you think Turnbridge Fitness Centre should launch at $25 per month using penetration pricing or open at the standard $42? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Launching at $25 per month would attract members quickly and undercut Capital Fitness's $45 price [k], helping Turnbridge close the gap from 240 members towards its target of 600 and fill the 1,500-capacity gym [app], building loyalty before the price rises to $42 after the 3-month offer [an]. However, an opening price of $42 would protect profit margins from day one [k], earning $17 more per member each month and repaying the $80,000 launch spend faster [app], preserving cash for running costs and new equipment [an]. Overall, the stronger position is penetration pricing at $25 for 3 months [eval], because the gym is only 4 months old and needs volume, habit and word of mouth to compete with Capital Fitness's 900 established members, and margins can be restored at $42 once loyalty is built [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Penetration launch undercuts rivals and drives quick volume
Standard opening protects margins and cash from day one
application_max_2: 240 members versus target of 600; 1,500 capacity; $25 undercuts Capital Fitness's $45
$42 earns $17 more per member; helps repay the $80,000 launch spend
analysis_max_2: Penetration builds loyalty and word of mouth before price rises to $42
Standard opening preserves cash for running costs and equipment
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation based on the gym being only 4 months old and needing volume and habit
Recognises Capital Fitness's 900 established members and weighs $17 per-member margin against growth speed

scenario_stem:
Vertex Drone Works is a private limited company in Country X founded 3 years ago by engineer-entrepreneur Lena Okafor. It designs camera drones for professional surveyors and employs 18 hardware engineers and flight technicians. Last year Vertex sold 1,100 drones at $1,500 each, earning $1.65 million revenue, with research and development spending of $220,000.

The flagship Vertex Pro X1 uses a survey-grade camera and was developed at a cost of $180,000. The board is choosing between price skimming at $2,400 per unit for the first 12 months, aimed at surveying firms and early adopters, or penetration pricing at $1,500 per unit to undercut rivals immediately. Pre-orders stand at 300 units at $2,400, and each Vertex Pro X1 costs $1,050 to produce. Lena wants the skimming launch; her sales director prefers the lower price.

questions.question_text: Define 'price skimming'.
questions.model_answer: Price skimming is a pricing method where a new product is launched at a high price to earn high profits from early adopters and recover development costs, before the price is lowered later as the product becomes established [2].

knowledge_max_2: New product launched at a high price
High profits earned early / price lowered later as product establishes

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of price skimming for Vertex Drone Works.
questions.model_answer: Price skimming generates high profits from customers willing to pay a premium [k], because each Vertex Pro X1 sold at $2,400 earns $1,350 above its $1,050 production cost [app]. It also helps recover the $180,000 development cost of the new model quickly [k], turning the 300 pre-orders at $2,400 into $720,000 of early revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: High profit per unit / high margins from premium buyers
Recovers research and development costs quickly
application_max_2: $2,400 price versus $1,050 production cost gives a $1,350 margin
300 pre-orders at $2,400 worth $720,000 towards the $180,000 development cost

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of price skimming for Vertex Drone Works.
questions.model_answer: A high launch price attracts fewer buyers in the wider market [k], since many surveying firms may wait for a lower price rather than pay $2,400 for the Vertex Pro X1 [app], limiting sales beyond the 300 pre-orders and slowing revenue growth [an]. Competitors may also copy the drone quickly [k], because a high price with strong early margins signals a profitable market [app], forcing Vertex to cut prices sooner and reducing the benefit of skimming [an].

knowledge_max_2: High price limits the number of buyers / appeals only to early adopters
High profit signals attract competitor entry and copying
application_max_2: $2,400 price for the Vertex Pro X1 may deter surveying firms outside the 300 pre-orders
Strength of margins invites rivals to copy, ending the skimming window in the first 12 months
analysis_max_2: Slower adoption limits early revenue and delays cost recovery
Earlier-than-planned price cuts erode the expected skimming benefit

questions.question_text: Do you think Vertex Drone Works should launch the Vertex Pro X1 at $2,400 using price skimming or at $1,500 using penetration pricing? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Price skimming at $2,400 would earn a $1,350 margin per unit [k], and the 300 pre-orders alone would deliver $720,000, helping recover the $180,000 development cost fast [app], funding future research and protecting Vertex's premium positioning through the first 12 months with early adopters [an]. However, penetration pricing at $1,500 would undercut rivals immediately [k], matching the company's volume drone already selling 1,100 units a year at $1,500 and protecting the $1.65 million revenue line [app], which reduces the risk of weak launch sales and speeds adoption [an]. Overall, the stronger choice is price skimming at $2,400 [eval], because Vertex's customers are professional surveyors who value survey-grade accuracy over price, and early adopters expect to pay a premium for a genuinely new flagship product [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Penetration undercuts rivals to win adoption quickly
Skimming earns premium margins from early adopters
application_max_2: 300 pre-orders at $2,400 worth $720,000 towards the $180,000 development cost; margin $1,350 per unit
1,100 drones a year already sold at $1,500; penetration matches the $1.65 million revenue line
analysis_max_2: Skimming funds future research and holds premium positioning for 12 months
Penetration cuts launch risk and speeds adoption but sacrifices margin
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation referencing the professional surveyor customer base and early adopters
Weighs survey-grade differentiation and pre-order evidence against the appeal of a lower launch price

scenario_stem:
Ambertide Resort & Spa is a private limited company in Country X, a 120-room beach resort with a spa and three restaurants, established 11 years ago by the Verma family. It employs 85 staff across operations, food and beverage, and maintenance. Peak-season occupancy, from December to April, reaches 85% at $220 per room per night, while off-peak occupancy, from June to September, falls to 45%.

To lift off-peak trade, general manager Ravi Verma proposes promotional pricing: a three-night package at $150 per night with breakfast included and a free dinner worth $45 for each stay, aimed at families. He estimates the promotion could raise off-peak occupancy from 45% to 70%, costing about $12,000 in advertising. Director Meera Verma prefers keeping the standard $220 rate to protect the resort's premium image and profit per room.

questions.question_text: Define 'promotional pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Promotional pricing is a pricing method where a business lowers its price for a limited time, or offers a special package or discount, to boost sales volume, often in a quiet period or to clear stock [2].

knowledge_max_2: Price is lowered for a limited time / special offer made
Aim is to boost sales volume, often in quiet periods or to clear stock

questions.question_text: Explain two aims of promotional pricing for Ambertide Resort & Spa.
questions.model_answer: Promotional pricing aims to increase sales during quiet periods [k], helping Ambertide lift off-peak occupancy from 45% towards the proposed 70% with its $150 three-night package [app]. It also aims to attract new customer groups such as families [k], using the free dinner worth $45 to make the deal more appealing [app].

knowledge_max_2: Increase sales / lift occupancy in a quiet period
Attract new customer groups to the business
application_max_2: Off-peak occupancy expected to rise from 45% to 70% with the three-night package
Free dinner worth $45 aimed at attracting families

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of promotional pricing for Ambertide Resort & Spa.
questions.model_answer: Selling rooms at $150 instead of the standard $220 reduces the profit earned per room per night [k], and breakfast and the free dinner worth $45 add further cost [app], so each guest contributes far less, weakening off-peak profit even if occupancy rises [an]. Frequent promotions also train customers to expect lower prices [k], as families wait for the deal rather than book at $220 [app], damaging the resort's premium image and long-run profit per room [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower price reduces profit per sale / margins are squeezed
Customers learn to expect discounts / brand image suffers
application_max_2: $150 package versus $220 standard rate; breakfast and a free dinner worth $45 add cost
Families may wait for the deal rather than book at $220
analysis_max_2: Weaker off-peak profit per room even if occupancy rises to 70%
Brand image damage reduces long-run pricing power and profit per room

questions.question_text: Do you think Ambertide Resort & Spa should run the promotional package ($150 per night with breakfast and a free dinner) or keep the standard $220 rate? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The promotional package would lift off-peak occupancy from 45% towards 70% [k], filling more of the 120 rooms in June to September, where occupancy is just 45% at the standard $220 rate [app], raising total room revenue and keeping staff busy through the quiet season [an]. However, keeping $220 protects the premium image and profit per room [k], avoiding over-reliance on discounts and the $12,000 advertising spend, and avoiding training families to expect deals [app], which protects long-term margin and brand strength [an]. Overall, the stronger position is to run the promotional package for the off-peak months only [eval], because 70% occupancy across 120 rooms (84 rooms) earns far more than 45% (54 rooms) at $220, even with the added $45 dinner cost [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Promotion fills rooms in quiet periods and attracts new customers
Keeping the standard rate protects premium image and margin
application_max_2: Off-peak occupancy 45% to 70%; 120 rooms (84 versus 54 rooms filled); $150 rate with breakfast
$220 standard rate; $12,000 advertising spend; free dinner worth $45 per stay
analysis_max_2: Higher occupancy raises total room revenue and covers staff through quiet months
Holding rate avoids deal-expectation and protects long-run margin and brand
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation weighting 84 rooms at $150 against 54 rooms at $220
Recognises the dinner cost ($45) and advertising ($12,000) but still favours the promotion

scenario_stem:
Crosswinds Airways is a private limited company in Country X operating short-haul flights to 14 destinations. Founded 7 years ago by the Sandoval family, it employs 260 staff including 90 pilots and cabin crew. Last year it carried 240,000 passengers at an average fare of $150, earning $36 million in revenue. Peak-weekend flights run at 82% occupancy, while off-peak midweek flights average 54%.

The board is considering replacing the flat $150 fare with dynamic pricing: fares could rise to $260 on busy flights 48 hours before departure and fall to as low as $89 on empty midweek flights, with demand-adjustment software costing $35,000 per year. Director Elena Sandoval worries that passengers dislike unpredictable fares and may switch to FaresAir, which charges a flat $140. Chairman Marco Sandoval argues dynamic pricing will fill off-peak seats and lift average fares.

questions.question_text: Define 'dynamic pricing'.
questions.model_answer: Dynamic pricing is a pricing method where prices are changed continuously in response to demand, supply and other market conditions, so the price differs between times, situations or customers [2].

knowledge_max_2: Prices are changed continuously in response to conditions
Price differs between times, situations or customers

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of dynamic pricing for Crosswinds Airways.
questions.model_answer: Dynamic pricing maximises revenue from passengers willing to pay more [k], lifting fares to as much as $260 on busy flights 48 hours before departure [app]. It also fills empty seats by lowering prices [k], with off-peak midweek fares falling to as low as $89 to attract price-sensitive passengers when occupancy averages 54% [app].

knowledge_max_2: Maximises revenue from passengers willing to pay more
Lowers price to fill empty seats / increase off-peak occupancy
application_max_2: Fares could rise to $260 on busy flights 48 hours before departure
Off-peak fares could fall to as low as $89 with occupancy at 54%

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of dynamic pricing for Crosswinds Airways.
questions.model_answer: Passengers may resent unpredictable fares [k], feeling overcharged close to departure when the fare may reach $260 instead of $150 [app], damaging loyalty and pushing flyers to FaresAir [an]. Dynamic pricing also requires investment and ongoing cost [k], such as the $35,000 per year demand-adjustment software [app], adding fixed cost that must be recouped across the 14 routes served [an].

knowledge_max_2: Passengers resent unpredictable or seemingly unfair fares
Requires investment in systems / ongoing software costs
application_max_2: Fares may jump from $150 to $260 near departure
$35,000 per year demand-adjustment software across 14 destinations
analysis_max_2: Loyalty damage pushes passengers to FaresAir's $140 flat fare
Software cost must be recouped, squeezing margins on weaker routes

questions.question_text: Do you think Crosswinds Airways should introduce dynamic pricing or keep the flat $150 fare? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Dynamic pricing would raise revenue where demand is highest [k], lifting fares to $260 on busy peak flights and to as low as $89 on empty midweek flights [app], so total fare revenue should rise above the current $36 million while 82% peak occupancy is monetised effectively [an]. However, the flat $150 fare is predictable and trusted [k], avoiding customer frustration and the risk that price-sensitive passengers switch to FaresAir, whose flat $140 is $10 cheaper [app], protecting Crosswinds' reputation on the 14 routes it serves [an]. Overall, the stronger position is to introduce dynamic pricing [eval], because peak flights at 82% occupancy are already selling out and fares should reflect that scarcity, while $89 off-peak fares will win new passengers that a flat $150 fare drives away [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Dynamic pricing monetises high-demand seats and fills empty ones
Flat fare is predictable and trusted by regular passengers
application_max_2: Peak fares to $260, off-peak to $89; revenue could exceed $36 million; 82% peak occupancy
FaresAir flat $140 is $10 cheaper; flat $150 predictable across 14 destinations
analysis_max_2: Higher peak fares monetise scarcity of seats at 82% occupancy
Flat fare protects reputation and avoids losing passengers to FaresAir
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation that selling-out peak flights should charge more
Weighs FaresAir switching risk and the flat $150's predictability against revenue gain

scenario_stem:
Copperhill Pharmacy is a private limited company in Country X, run by owners Ade and Ruth Boateng for 5 years. It has 2 branches and employs 11 pharmacists and assistants, generating $1.1 million in annual revenue, of which $600,000 comes from prescription medicines. A large supermarket pharmacy chain operates 500 metres from the main branch.

Demand for prescription pain relief is price-inelastic: customers must fill prescriptions and few leave over small rises. Demand for vitamins, shampoos and cold remedies is price-elastic: many substitutes exist and a small rise can cut sales sharply. Ruth wants to raise the price of a common prescription medicine from $12.50 to $13.50, an 8% rise. Ade prefers holding prescription prices and instead discounting vitamins by 10% from $9.00 to $8.10 to win price-sensitive shoppers from the supermarket rival.

questions.question_text: Define 'price-elastic demand'.
questions.model_answer: Price-elastic demand is when demand for a product is sensitive to price changes: a small rise in price leads to a relatively large fall in quantity demanded, and a small fall leads to a relatively large rise in demand [2].

knowledge_max_2: Demand is sensitive to price changes
Small price rise causes a larger fall in quantity demanded (and vice versa)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why demand for prescription medicines at Copperhill Pharmacy is price-inelastic.
questions.model_answer: Prescription medicines are necessities for patients [k], so customers must fill their prescriptions even if Copperhill raises a common pain relief from $12.50 to $13.50 [app]. There are few close substitutes for many prescribed drugs [k], so the 2 branches lose very few of the $600,000 in prescription sales when prices rise slightly [app].

knowledge_max_2: Prescription medicines are necessities
Few close substitutes for prescribed drugs
application_max_2: $12.50 to $13.50 rise (8%) on a common pain relief
Little risk to the $600,000 of prescription revenue across the 2 branches

questions.question_text: Explain two factors that make demand for the vitamins sold by Copperhill Pharmacy price-elastic.
questions.model_answer: Vitamins have many close substitutes available [k], since supermarkets and the large chain 500 metres away also sell competing brands [app], so a small price rise can send Copperhill's vitamin customers elsewhere [an]. Vitamins are also non-essential purchases that customers cut back on easily [k], so a 10% discount from $9.00 to $8.10 would likely draw in price-sensitive shoppers [app], increasing vitamin sales volume and footfall into the 2 branches [an].

knowledge_max_2: Many close substitutes exist for vitamins
Vitamins are non-essential / customers can postpone or switch purchases
application_max_2: Supermarket and the large chain 500 metres from the main branch sell competing brands
Proposed 10% discount from $9.00 to $8.10 to win price-sensitive shoppers
analysis_max_2: Small price change shifts demand to rivals, so volume falls sharply
Discounting pulls in shoppers, lifting vitamin sales and store footfall

questions.question_text: Do you think Copperhill Pharmacy should raise the price of the common prescription medicine to $13.50, or hold prescription prices and discount vitamins to $8.10? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising the prescription price to $13.50 (an 8% rise) would raise revenue without losing many customers [k], because essential prescription demand is price-inelastic and few patients will change pharmacy over a $1.00 rise [app], lifting the $600,000 prescription line across the 2 branches [an]. However, holding prescription prices and cutting vitamins by 10% to $8.10 would attract price-sensitive shoppers from the competing chain 500 metres away [k], competing on a range where demand is price-elastic [app], lifting footfall and the chance that customers buy higher-margin over-the-counter goods as well [an]. Overall, the stronger position is to hold prescription prices and discount the vitamins [eval], because an 8% rise on an inelastic essential risks customer trust and community goodwill, while winning elastic, everyday shoppers defends Copperhill's total $1.1 million revenue across both branches [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Inelastic essentials can bear a price rise without losing many customers
Elastic goods respond to discounts, attracting price-sensitive shoppers
application_max_2: $12.50 to $13.50, an 8% rise; $600,000 prescription revenue across 2 branches
Vitamins cut 10% from $9.00 to $8.10; supermarket chain 500 metres away
analysis_max_2: Price rise lifts the protected prescription revenue with minimal volume loss
Discounting lifts footfall and cross-selling of higher-margin goods
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation weighting trust on an inelastic essential against elastic everyday shoppers
Weighs $1.1 million total revenue across both branches, not just the prescription line

scenario_stem:
Sable & Sparrow Fashion is a private limited company in Country Z specialising in winter coats, founded 6 years ago by owner Freya Lindqvist. It has 2 stores and employs 12 sales assistants, generating $980,000 in annual revenue. Each winter coat costs $60 to buy and sells at $90, a 50% markup. As spring approaches, 600 coats remain unsold, and storage costs $2 per coat per month, $1,200 in total.

Freya is considering promotional pricing: a 25% end-of-season discount, falling to $67.50, which still covers the $60 cost with $7.50 profit per coat. Her partner favours holding the standard $90 price to protect the brand's premium image, though up to 40% of the 600 coats may remain unsold by next winter. scenario_stem:
Pinnacle Audio Labs is a private limited company in Country Y founded 2 years ago by founder Theo Mensah, designing wireless headphones for commuters. It employs 9 product designers and engineers and has spent $120,000 developing its noise-cancelling Aria headphones. Production costs are $140 per unit and 1,500 pre-orders have been received at the proposed $399 launch price.

A rival, SoundWave, sells a similar headphone at $249, undercutting Pinnacle's plan by $150. The board must choose between price skimming at $399, capturing early adopters before competitors respond, or a competitive $249 to match SoundWave and win share from day one. At $399 the margin is $259 per unit; at $249 the margin is $109. Sales director Ivy Brooks prefers $249, while Theo believes the headphones' battery life justifies the premium.

scenario_stem:
Quayside Ferry Co is a private limited company in Country Z, running commuter ferries across the Kessler Strait since 2018. It employs 46 crew and office staff and carries 500,000 passengers a year, with revenue of $6.0 million at a flat $12 fare. Peak-hour occupancy is 88%, off-peak services run at just 38%, and fuel costs have risen by 25% this year.

The board proposes dynamic pricing: peak fares would rise to $15 and off-peak fares fall to $9, adjusted by demand. Director Colin Reyes estimates revenue would reach $6.3 million, with 300,000 peak passengers at $15 and 200,000 off-peak at $9, and software to run the system costs $40,000 a year. His colleague favours keeping the flat $12 fare because regular commuters dislike variable prices and may switch to the rival speedboat service, which charges $13.

questions.question_text: State two reasons why a business might charge different fares at peak and off-peak times.
questions.model_answer: Two reasons are: to earn more revenue from passengers travelling at busy times, and to spread demand by encouraging off-peak travel with lower fares [2].

knowledge_max_2: Earn more revenue from busy-time passengers
Spread demand / encourage off-peak travel with lower fares

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of dynamic pricing for Quayside Ferry Co.
questions.model_answer: Dynamic pricing raises fares when demand is highest [k], lifting peak fares to $15 while off-peak fares fall to $9 [app], so Quayside can monetise the 88% peak occupancy more effectively. It also encourages off-peak travel with lower fares [k], which can lift off-peak occupancy from its 38% level [app].

Lower prices encourage off-peak travel / spread demand
application_max_2: Peak fares $15 and off-peak $9, versus 88% peak occupancy

questions.model_answer: Regular commuters may resent fares changing between journeys [k], especially if peak fares reach $15, $3 above the current flat $12 [app], damaging loyalty among the 500,000 annual passengers and pushing them towards the rival speedboat at $13 [an]. Dynamic pricing also requires investment and ongoing cost [k], such as the $40,000 per year software licence [app], which must be paid even if off-peak demand stays at 38% occupancy [an].

Requires investment in systems / ongoing software cost

questions.question_text: Do you think Quayside Ferry Co should introduce dynamic pricing ($15 peak, $9 off-peak) or keep the flat $12 fare? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Dynamic pricing would raise total revenue from $6.0 million to $6.3 million [k], based on 300,000 peak passengers at $15 and 200,000 off-peak passengers at $9 [app], adding $300,000 that would more than cover the $40,000 software cost and offset the 25% fuel increase [an]. However, keeping the flat $12 fare protects predictability for regular commuters [k], avoiding the risk that they switch to the rival speedboat service at $13, which is only $1 more if peak fares rise to $15 [app], protecting Quayside's reputation and existing passenger base [an]. Overall, the stronger position is dynamic pricing [eval], because peak occupancy is 88% and fares should reflect that scarcity, while $9 off-peak fares will win price-sensitive passengers without abandoning peak revenue [eval].

Flat fare is predictable and protects loyalty
